summary: This document extends DLEP with a credit window scheme aware of IEEE 802.1Q for Ethernet, supporting destination-specific and shared flow control. It builds on the base DLEP credit window mechanism.

eli5.summary: Ethernet traffic can be labeled with priority tags. This gives each tag its own tickets so flow can be controlled fairly.

questions: what is dlep ethernet credit extension
how does dlep flow control work
subtitle: How DLEP modems and routers can meter Ethernet traffic with credit windows tied to VLANs and priority bits.

tldr.problem: The Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) lets a router and a modem swap link information, but it defines no flow control, so a router has no standard way to hold back Ethernet traffic the modem cannot yet carry.
tldr.mechanism: This extension reuses the traffic classification and credit window machinery of RFC 9892 and RFC 9893, and keys credit windows on DLEP destination, VLAN identifier and 802.1Q Priority Code Point, with wildcards allowed.
tldr.outcome: A router MUST NOT send to the modem unless credits are available. Support is announced with Extension Type value 5, and the RFC recommends avoiding wildcards unless clearly needed.

today: RFC 9895 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2026, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is one of a group of DLEP documents, alongside RFC 9892, RFC 9893 and RFC 9894.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP, RFC 8175) carries link-related control information between two peers, a modem and a router. DLEP defines a base set of mechanisms plus support for extensions. It does not define any flow control, and this document adds one as an extension.

The extension introduces an Ethernet-based flow control mechanism for traffic sent from the router to the modem. It uses one or more logical credit windows, each typically tied to a virtual or physical queue. The router uses traffic classification information supplied by the modem to pick the right credit window for a flow.

The extension is called the IEEE 802.1Q Aware Credit Window extension, or more simply the Ethernet Credit extension. Readers are expected to know the classification and credit mechanisms of RFC 9892 and RFC 9893.
sections.eli5: A router and a radio box talk to each other. This document gives them a ticket system so the router only sends as much as the box can take.

sections.title: Credit Windows, VLANs and Priorities
sections.content:
The extension builds on RFC 9892 and RFC 9893 to give credit-window flow control based on DLEP destinations, Ethernet Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs) and Priority Code Points (PCPs). The IEEE 802.1Q tag format carries a 3-bit PCP field and a 12-bit VLAN Identifier (VID) field.

A credit window can be shared across traffic for several DLEP destinations, VLANs and PCPs, or dedicated to the traffic of one destination, VLAN and/or PCP. The extension also supports wildcard matching for any PCP or VID.

For a Diffserv-based approach to credit windows, the RFC points to RFC 9894. When both Diffserv and Ethernet classification apply to a flow, Ethernet-based classification takes precedence, as set out in Section 2.3.1 of RFC 9892.
sections.eli5: Each kind of Ethernet label can get its own pile of tickets, or several labels can share one pile. A special wildcard label means any label at all.

sections.title: Announcing the Extension
sections.content:
To use the extension, an implementation MUST include the IEEE 802.1Q Aware Credit Window Extension Type value in the Extensions Supported Data Item defined in Section 13.6 of RFC 8175. That item is sent and processed as RFC 8175 describes. The Extension Type value is 5.

An implementation that signals the extension MUST support all message types, Data Items, the Ethernet Traffic Classification Sub-Data Item and the related processing defined in RFC 9892 and RFC 9893.
sections.eli5: Before using the ticket system, each side says so out loud, using the number 5. If you say you play, you must know all the rules.

sections.title: Management Considerations
sections.content:
Support for the extension MUST be declared with the Extensions Supported Data Item, which is configurable on both modems and routers. Use of the extension SHOULD be configurable on both sides. The extension's Data Items MUST NOT be emitted unless support was specified in the initialization message received from the peer.

Modems SHOULD support mapping a PCP to a credit window (queue) and MAY support doing so per VLAN. In traffic classification, VID 0x0000 means the VID is ignored, 0xFFFF is reserved, and values 0x0001 through 0xFFFE can be used. A modem that supports VLANs without PCPs SHOULD support mapping a VLAN to a credit window. Modems MAY let the operator configure how many credit windows they advertise.

Routers may be limited in the queues they can support, and per-destination queues may not be available. If the modem advertises more than the router can handle, the router SHOULD use a subset of the advertised windows, or MAY reset the session and indicate that the extension is not supported. Either way, the mismatch SHOULD be reported through standard network management means such as a user interface notice or an error log.

Whatever the implementation, when credit windows are in use the router MUST NOT send traffic to the modem unless sufficient credits are available.
sections.eli5: The modem decides how many piles of tickets there are. If the router cannot handle that many, it uses only some of them, or starts over, and tells a person about it. It never sends without a ticket.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension relies on DLEP and on the credit window mechanisms of RFC 9892 and RFC 9893, whose security sections also apply. It is exposed to threats like those against existing DLEP messages, for example an injected message that resizes a credit window to a value causing denial of service. The security mechanisms of RFC 8175 can be applied equally here.

Wildcards for PCP and VID fields can be convenient, but they could inadvertently match unexpected flows, or new flows that appear after the wildcard was set up. The RFC therefore RECOMMENDS that wildcards not be used unless clearly needed.
sections.eli5: A trickster could send a fake message that shrinks the pile of tickets. Also, a wildcard label can grab more traffic than you meant, so use it only when you must.

sections.title: IANA Code Point
sections.content: IANA has assigned code 5, described as "IEEE 802.1Q Aware Credit Window", in the Extension Type Values registry within the Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) Parameters registry group. No other registrations are made.
sections.eli5: The official list of extension numbers now has an entry, number 5, for this one.

viz.caption: WHAT A CREDIT WINDOW CAN BE KEYED ON

items.title: DLEP destination
items.text: Traffic for one destination or for several.

items.title: VLAN (VID)
items.text: A 12-bit VLAN Identifier; a wildcard can match any VID.

items.title: Priority (PCP)
items.text: A 3-bit Priority Code Point; a wildcard can match any PCP.

items.title: Shared or dedicated
items.text: One window for many flows, or one window per flow.
